notes.title: Risk register RR-118 — TechFlow log retention
notes.content:
Finding: VR-2027-004. Vendor retains customer identifiers in application logs for 90 days hot plus 275 days archive, against a 30-day policy maximum.

Decision: ACCEPTED with conditions, 12 March 2027.

Conditions:
1. Pilot remains on de-identified data until the identifier-hashing change ships.
2. TechFlow implements one-way hashing of all customer identifiers at log write, verified by evidence, by 30 June 2027.
3. Archive retention reduced to 90 days total by the same date.

Compensating control: pilot scope excludes production clinical data; Privacy determination D-2027-11 is the binding constraint until the BAA executes.

Expiry: 31 July 2027. If conditions are unmet the exception lapses and the pilot stops.

What may be told to the vendor: that an exception exists, its conditions, and its expiry. Not the reasoning, not the compensating-control analysis, not what else was on the table.

notes.title: Exception log — open items
notes.content:
Four open exceptions:
- RR-118 TechFlow log retention — expires 31 Jul 2027
- RR-101 legacy scheduling cluster, unsupported OS — expires 30 Sep 2027, third renewal
- RR-109 shared service account, imaging archive — expires 30 Jun 2027
- RR-114 deferred MFA for two clinical kiosks — expires 30 Apr 2027

Two expire this quarter. RR-101 is the one I am least comfortable renewing again; the compensating controls have not changed in eighteen months.

notes.title: KH-SEC-04 — third-party data handling standard
notes.content:
Published standard. Key clauses vendors are told about directly:
- Customer identifiers in vendor logs: maximum 30 days retention
- Encryption at rest and in transit required, with a documented key rotation schedule
- No shared administrative accounts for production access
- Formal access re-certification at least every 90 days
- Security incident notification to Kestrel within 24 hours of vendor awareness

Exceptions require a compensating control and a stated expiry. There is no permanent exception.

notes.title: Exception request process
notes.content:
An exception requires: the finding, the business justification, a proposed compensating control, a remediation plan with dates, and a named owner. Requests without an expiry date are returned unread.

Only the CISO grants an exception. Neither the SOC nor IT leadership can, and neither can a vendor's assurance that a control is 'effectively equivalent'.

notes.title: Security programme status — Q1 board summary
notes.content:
Reported to the Board IT Committee, 4 March.
- Vendor reviews completed this quarter: 6
- Open exceptions: 4, all with expiry dates
- Reportable incidents: 0
- Control maturity self-assessment: 3.2 of 5, up from 2.9

No detail on findings or affected systems in the board pack. That is deliberate.

notes.title: Note to self — the pattern in RR-118
notes.content:
The vendor keeps framing the log retention as a security control question. Grace is right that it becomes a privacy question the moment the pilot touches live data, and the two determinations have different owners and different tests.

My exception does not authorise a disclosure. It is not mine to authorise. If anyone reads RR-118 as clearing the vendor to receive identifiable data, that is a misreading I should pre-empt in writing.

notes.title: Security programme — FY27 plan
notes.content:
Three priorities: medical device segmentation, identity governance, and third-party assurance.

Segmentation is the one that reduces the most risk and the one with the least visible progress, which is a communication problem I have not solved.

notes.title: Board reporting — what actually lands
notes.content:
Four slides. Incidents, programme status, exceptions, and one thing I want them to remember.

The fourth slide is the only one that changes behaviour. This quarter it is the clinical downtime decision gap.

notes.title: Cyber insurance renewal
notes.content:
Renewal in June. The questionnaire is longer than last year and asks about medical device patching, which is our weakest number.

Answering it honestly will cost premium. Answering it any other way is not an option.

notes.title: Identity governance — business case
notes.content:
Joiner-mover-leaver is manual and it fails at 'mover' every time. Eleven stale accounts found in the last reconciliation.

Business case drafted. It competes against clinical systems for the same capital and it will lose, again, and it should not.

notes.title: Security policy set — review cycle
notes.content:
Fourteen policies, annual review, staggered so we are not rewriting everything in one month. Four due this quarter.

Most reviews change nothing, which is fine — the point is that someone read it.

notes.title: Incident response retainer
notes.content:
External IR firm on retainer, four hours guaranteed response. Exercised once in two years and they were good.

The retainer is the cheapest thing in my budget and the hardest to justify to someone reading a spreadsheet.

notes.title: Segmentation programme — where it is stuck
notes.content:
Design complete. Implementation blocked on a device inventory that is 60% accurate, because you cannot segment what you cannot see.

So the inventory is the programme, and it does not look like a security project, which is why it is hard to fund.

notes.title: Risk appetite — the conversation we have not had
notes.content:
The board has never stated a risk appetite, which means every exception I grant is measured against my own judgement rather than an agreed line.

That works until it does not. Raising it makes me look like I want cover, and I partly do.

notes.title: Third-party assurance — programme view
notes.content:
Sixty vendors with some level of access. Twenty assessed in the last two years. The other forty are assessed by the fact that nothing has gone wrong yet.

That is not assurance, it is luck with a process wrapped round it.

notes.title: Exception hygiene
notes.content:
Every exception has a compensating control and an expiry. No exception is permanent.

I have inherited three that were effectively permanent because they were renewed without review. Those are now the ones I look at first.

notes.title: Security team — headcount
notes.content:
Three including me. The sector benchmark for this size is five to seven.

We cover it by being selective about what we do, which means the things we do not do are invisible until they matter.

notes.title: Security programme roadmap — FY27
notes.content: Three priorities: medical device segmentation, third-party lifecycle, and identity. Everything else is maintenance. The board pack shows all three as amber and two of them will stay amber.

notes.title: Medical device segmentation — status
notes.content: 280 of 412 devices segmented. The remaining 132 are governed by clinical engineering and move at their pace, not mine. This is the largest unaccepted risk in the register and it has no expiry date, which by my own rule it should.

notes.title: Policy set — annual review
notes.content: Nineteen policies, six due for review this year. Most changes are minor. The third-party standard is the one that generates argument every time.

notes.title: Identity programme — MFA coverage
notes.content: MFA on 94% of accounts. The 6% is clinical kiosks and two service accounts. RR-114 covers the kiosks and expires in April, for the third time.

notes.title: Why every exception has an expiry
notes.content: An exception without an expiry is a policy change made by someone without the authority to change policy. Requests arriving without one are returned unread, and people stop leaving it off after the first time.

notes.title: Regional CISO group — notes
notes.content: Quarterly. Everyone has the same three problems: medical devices, third parties, and not enough analysts. Two systems in the group had ransomware in the last eighteen months and both started with a vendor.

notes.title: Risk register — the shape of it
notes.content: Forty-one entries. Four open exceptions. The register is honest, which means it is uncomfortable to read, which means most people have not read it.

notes.title: Tabletop findings — last year
notes.content: Clinical downtime procedures existed on paper and nobody on the units had seen them. That was the finding and it was worth the whole exercise.

notes.title: Security in the capital plan
notes.content: Security competes with clinical equipment and always loses on emotional weight. The only argument that works is regulatory, which is why the interoperability mandate is quietly useful to me.

notes.title: Phishing — why the click rate is the wrong metric
notes.content: Click rate measures curiosity. Credential submission measures the actual failure. Reporting rate measures whether the programme is working. We report all three and the board looks at the first.

notes.title: Exception RR-109 — imaging shared account
notes.content: A shared service account on the imaging archive. Vendor says it cannot be split. Expires June and I do not believe the vendor.

notes.title: Restore test — restricted security annex
notes.content: The restricted annex contains recovery credentials and unmitigated infrastructure weaknesses. Continuity and clinical owners receive the failed capability, fallback, risk owner and retest result without credential material.
